name: The Broken Window Fallacy
aliases: The parable of the broken window
That which is seen and that which is not seen
statement: Destruction is not wealth: the spending it forces only diverts what would have been spent elsewhere.
statementAccent: the spending it forces only diverts
meaning: The broken window fallacy is the error of thinking that destruction is economically beneficial because it generates work and spending. When a shopkeeper's window is broken, the glazier gains work, and it is tempting to conclude the accident did some good. The fallacy is to count only this visible activity while ignoring the unseen: the money spent on the repair can no longer be spent on something else. Destruction creates no net wealth; it merely diverts resources and leaves society poorer by the value of what was destroyed.
mechanism: The reasoning turns on opportunity cost, the value of the alternative that a choice forecloses. What is seen is the glazier receiving his fee and business being stimulated, an immediate and visible gain. What is not seen is that the shopkeeper, having spent on the window, cannot now spend on shoes or a book he would otherwise have bought, and the value that purchase would have added never appears. The window is merely restored to what it was, at the cost of new goods never made, so measured activity rises while the stock of real wealth falls.

examples.text: A careless boy breaks a shopkeeper's pane and a glazier is paid six francs to replace it; the onlookers cheer the business created, forgetting the six francs the shopkeeper can no longer spend elsewhere.
The claim that a hurricane or a war 'stimulates' the economy by requiring rebuilding is the same fallacy: rebuilding only restores lost wealth and diverts resources from new production.
Bastiat's lesson is that the bad economist sees only the immediate visible effect while the good economist also reckons the effects that must be foreseen but are not seen.

variants.name: Wealth versus activity
variants.text: The underlying distinction between wealth, the stock of valuable goods a society holds, and activity, the transactions and employment it generates; breaking the window raises activity but lowers wealth.

variants.name: The recession qualification
variants.text: A debated case in which, in a deep slump with idle labour and capital, extra spending may raise output because the unseen alternative use is not fully crowded out, though even here destruction of existing wealth is not held to be desirable.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational teaching example for opportunity cost and for the discipline of tracing second-order, unseen effects rather than stopping at the visible ones. It is the central organising idea of Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson', one of the most widely circulated works of popular economics, and it is invoked whenever commentators claim that war, disaster, or wasteful spending will boost the economy. Its lasting value is as a habit of mind: always ask what the resources would otherwise have done.

working.text: when a policy or event 'creates work', ask what the resources would otherwise have produced, and subtract that foregone value.
distinguish a rise in measured activity from a rise in real wealth, since destruction can raise the first while lowering the second.
treat arguments that catastrophe boosts the economy with suspicion, since rebuilding restores rather than adds to wealth.

limits: The parable is a pedagogical argument about opportunity cost, not a claim that destruction changes nothing measurable; it shows destruction cannot be a net source of wealth. At the margins there is genuine debate: some economists argue that in a deep recession with idle resources, additional spending can raise output because the unseen alternative would otherwise sit idle, so the strict 'no benefit' conclusion is contested in that special case. Even then the debate is about whether spending can be stimulative, not whether destruction is good, and overstating it into 'Bastiat was wrong' misrepresents both sides.
misreadings: It is not the same as the broken windows theory of criminology, which is an unrelated idea sharing only the metaphor, about how visible disorder invites more disorder. It does not prove that all government or public spending is wasteful; it concerns the accounting of destruction and opportunity cost, not the merits of any particular programme. And it is not the claim that repair work is worthless; the point is that the window was already there, so society merely regains what it lost while forgoing something new.
origin: Set out by the French economist Frederic Bastiat in his 1850 essay 'Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas' ('That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen'), his last work, and later popularised by Henry Hazlitt in 'Economics in One Lesson' (1946).
